Then, what herald or embassy would ever come to need a man who was an orator, if it had been shown that counselling the people what seems good to the multitudes belongs to the orators? For what city, in sending an embassy, would choose to court a man worth nothing, or what envoy, on arrival, would ever have approached him for the sake of persuading the people, if he knew that the sum of the orator's life was to counsel whatever the people wished, and to wait for that man's voice as children, I think, wait for their teachers'? The case would have been the reverse of what it is with choruses, if the many were not going to wait for the orator, but the orator held back until the people gave their sign. And who, defending a private or public suit, would have sought one of the orators by whom he might win, if the orator was going to say what seemed good to the judges, and nothing else whatever? Thus those most in danger, and contending about the greatest matters, would most of all have neglected the orators. For there are those who are surely most in danger, for whom the dispositions of the hearers are difficult, and those who are prejudged by slanders. And if

the orators had made it their business to say what seemed good to the hearers, and exalted these things — Heracles! — a man might have carried his ruin from home, if anyone brought an orator to such a matter, just as if a man should bring in the executioner along with himself. Is it so, then, and do those who most expect to die, and on whom lies the greatest fear that they will not obtain a fair hearing, neglect the orators in any special degree? It is not so. Plato will not say things so paradoxical. Rather, they come to their doors, beg, grovel, thinking rhetoric a remedy for all things — death, exile, the fears themselves, the anger of judges, the contentiousness of the people, all. Why? Because they know that the orators do not practise saying what seems good to those sitting in judgment — for they could not even be said to practise this, if they were going to do that — but they know that the orators from afar attend to the matters and practise speaking as the order of the matters demands, aiming at the nature of these, not at the nature of the hearers; or if also at the nature of the hearers, yet not so as to serve their desires, nor to say all that they wish to hear, but to be able to persuade them by saying what is better to say — just as we see physicians too aiming at the nature of bodies, yet not so as simply to gratify desires, but so as not to apply the best thing at random, but in such a way as the patient will best accept it. To this extent I too say that the orator aims at the hearers, and if you say this, I agree; but not, I think, as a slave to the multitudes, nor for the sake of gratification does he observe their natures, but, as Demosthenes says, "that he may say the best things to the purpose." "I, for my part," he says, "am not at a loss what to say about the present matters, but in what manner I ought to speak to you about them." Then he uses frankness, and very

brilliantly, as I think. "For I am persuaded, from what I have seen and heard while present, that most matters have escaped you through your not wishing to do what is needful, not through your not understanding." If this is aiming, O Plato — to converse while watching the natures — we do not escape the charges, all the orators will say. But if you say that they yield to the multitudes and do what they are bidden, but do not bid, you have taken the handmaid for the mistress, and you seem to be censuring the public slaves, not the orators. But neither do the public slaves think highly of themselves because they serve the wishes of the city, and for the orators the very cause of their pride is this: that they do not say what seems good to the peoples, but what they themselves think best. And if they were servants of the desire of the crowds and declaimed what seemed good to those sitting in judgment, it would not even be possible for them to use frankness, much less to think above the rest. But, I think, they are conscious to themselves that they do not serve pleasures, but bring desires to soberness; that they do not look to the many, but the many look to them; that they are not ruled by the private men, but rule the many; and they have received their title from them, as a token instead of any other, a witness of their authority — I mean the title of "demagogues," not because they are led by the peoples, O you who turn everything upside down, but because they lead the peoples; just as we call them "pedagogues," I think, not because they have submitted to the children, but because they lead them. For whatever you say fits the orator to be called — ruler, champion, teacher: all these are names of the orator. For what teachers are to children, that the orators are to the peoples: they show what must be done, and instruct them by their counsels and decrees. And nature has so ordered these things. The chorus-leader does not serve the desires of the chorus-singers, but if he gratifies them in anything, he watches, along with his gratification, that nothing be sung amiss.

But the chorus-singers do not prompt him with the cues, nor does he, as they bid, apply the melody and the rhythm; nor does he learn from them what he must teach them — no more than the pilot learns from the sailors what must be done. Rather, the sailors hear what he commands, and the pilot says, not whatever seems good to the sailors, but whatever he, being himself in command of the sailors on the ship, judges. Everywhere all things look to the leaders, and their wishes lead the way. And the wishes of the many follow, some willingly, some unwillingly. The chorus-leader leads the chorus, the pilot the sailors, the general the soldiers, the orator the people. All rulers, then, are by nature superior to those under them; but if a man, having authority, also gratifies — persuading, not compelling — and, besides preserving his own rank, aims also at the desire of those under him, this is the man who is truly the statesman, and whom Homer said was "gentle as a father." And I think he made the same man the best orator too, to whom he attributed this. Do not, then, say this as a reproach against the orators, that they gratify, but only if they gratify apart from the best; if they aim at the best together with the gratification, then in this respect render to rhetoric her fitting praise, that you may be seen requiting her with like for like. But if you say that they simply gratify and serve desires, what is the proof? For I, from the very facts, furnish the other view. For if the orators were not going to be so admired, either by the peoples or by the private men or the citizens or the strangers, nor themselves at all to enjoy the dignities they now enjoy — in a word, if they were neither going to be esteemed, nor to make money, nor to have power, nor to speak — how is it possible to accept such a charge against them, through which these results would have followed? Then again, he has charged them with what is wholly

impossible. For perhaps it is not easy to gratify even the Centaurs, if one were addressing them — I do not mean all in common, but not even, I think, one by one, if their nature was double; but to know and serve the wishes of a people to the end — what device is there? And where is it possible? For there is no one people, nor of one desire — nor, I think, will there ever be; but, like streams, one is borne from one quarter and another from another, divided among all things — by ages, by pursuits, by natures, by fortune, by desires — one knowing one thing, another another, if indeed one ought to call "knowing" the knowing nothing whatever about the truth. And, by Zeus, some are present now, others next, like the leaves, which seem to be the same and of the same trees, but are never what they were before. By what desires, then, is the orator going to be a slave, or whose opinions is he to speak, or whom is he to aim at, who are so strangely disposed that they cannot themselves know what they wish? But they are so far from thinking the same things as one another that none of them, so to speak, thinks the same things to the end about the same matters even with himself, but all, using the orator as a guide of the hand, are always in need. At whom, then, tell me, will he look? For I will ask the same question again. And how will he serve their desires? For when he must serve many, and these are not of the same mind, and it is impossible to gratify all from the same things, how will the orator serve their desires? For at the same time he will gratify the one set and grieve the other. So that he will speak no more toward pleasure than toward displeasure. How, then, do you call these men servants? For it is not possible. And that Plato himself has agreed that the orators do not say what seems good to the many, one may, I suppose, point this out, that even a child attending would detect it — I say "detect," that I may not say "refute." For he grants this much, that rhetoric is the

craftsman of persuasion; and whether of belief or of teaching I do not now dispute — but at least he attributes persuading to her. When, then, persuading belongs to rhetoric, the orators do not say what seems good to the many. For if they say what already seems good, they do not persuade; for no one who has formed his own opinion is persuaded by another about this. But by this is distinguished the deliberating for oneself from being persuaded. But if indeed this too must be said, those who do what seems good to themselves are persuaded by themselves, not by the orators. And no one persuades who has not prevailed by speaking his own judgment. So that the very opposite of Plato's argument follows, if the orators say what seems good to the many. For what those who wish say, this they are persuaded to say. Therefore, if rhetoric is the craftsman of persuasion, and persuading belongs to the orators, the orators do not flatter; for they do not serve the many, but persuade them. But if the orators say what seems good to the many, rhetoric is not the craftsman of persuasion; for it presents men persuaded by the many, not persuading. In view of this, choose on which side the falsehood lies. For Plato refutes Plato for us — and, what is finest, not from afar, but from the same place and in the same arguments interwoven. That rhetoric, then, is neither irrational, nor such, so to speak, as merely to aim; nor, if it has a share of art, is this to be made a windfall; nor is it among the many arts I just went through, but, having the greatest share of reason — or rather wholly consisting in reasonings — and being the greatest and first of human things and the most perfect, and the very limit, if one may say so, of what one could pray for

— this is the thing to show. And one might know it if one considered her nature, and for what and how great things she was first discovered, and what she does and accomplishes throughout. I think, then, that all who are able would agree that men are not born in the same fashion, but in two divisions: one such as to use force and to grasp for more — which one would call the division of the stronger (I mean not the better in virtue, but the more powerful) — and the other such as to be worsted and to yield against its judgment, for want of power to prevent — which we recognize as belonging to the weaker. This, then, was what made men discover some such thing on their own behalf — or rather the gods discover it on behalf of men — which would restrain the strength, and would become for all, as it were, a pledge of the equal and the just, profitable alike to the many and to those by nature inclined to force. For not even those men were going to escape the recompense of unjust and evil deeds; rather, the weakest being first destroyed, and others by others little by little, and the rest being thus continually taken away, it remained for them, in the end, to come upon themselves — as they say the Sown Men did, if indeed the myth too hints at this. For to me, if one may digress, it seems wonderfully to wish to make this clear. He has made the beginning of their birth from a dragon's teeth, and says that the men themselves came up armed, and that Ares, instead of Hermes, had charge of that harvest. As I said, then, not even to those who surpass in powers was the seeming good fortune of the start going to profit in the end, but by the very thing in which they were stronger — or rather thought themselves to be — by this it remained for them to perish, so that the affairs of all men would utterly waste away. There was need, then, that some common remedy be found for the race, the same and profitable to all — to the strong, to the weaker, to the fair-minded — so as either to prevent some before their crimes,

or to punish at the very moment, and to provide for others a security of life, and for those who honoured justice willingly the fitting gratitude. There was discovered, then, out of these things, rhetoric, and she came forth as the guardian of justice and the bond of life for men, that affairs might be judged neither by hands, nor by arms, nor by being beforehand, nor by number and magnitude, nor by any other of the inequalities, but that reason might decide the just in tranquillity. This, then, is the origin and nature of rhetoric, and this her purpose — to save all men and to thrust back violence by persuasion. And, discovered for such and so great things, she alone has made our life worth living, bringing both private households and the common affairs of cities, so far as in her lies, into concord, establishing teaching and learning as forever a fine thing for all, and being the first to teach men everywhere to flee and hate unreason and tumults.

Let us consider, then, the laws too — what it is that made them — and if anyone finds another origin of laws, not the same as that of rhetoric, let him say this is nonsense, and win. But surely all would say this: that we needed laws for no other single thing than to suffer nothing grievous from one another, and that the base and bold should not prevail over the good, but the good should be superior to the base, together with justice. These are, so to speak, the two chief points of the laws: punishment of the unjust and honour of the fair. For if each obtained his deserts, there is no way in which justice could better be preserved, nor in which the common life of men could more securely be maintained. These things, then, appear to be present in the nature of rhetoric. For those for whom it sufficed to grasp for more in silence were not, I suppose, going to need speech — neither so as to win by speaking themselves (for they were strong elsewhere), nor so as to hear others; for this very thing was their wish, to hear no one. But those for whom there was no

other way to obtain equal terms had need of the speech that persuades; and this, again, was at once on behalf of justice. For the man who entrusts to himself and his resources what seems good to himself claims to prevail, of whatever sort it may be; but the man who looks to that by which he must also persuade those outside, and thinks fit to practise this, does not flee the test of what sort the things he wishes are. Rhetoric, then, appears to share the same nature with legislation, if indeed one must view the matter precisely in both cases — or rather legislation is a part of rhetoric, and in all respects, in a way, second to it. First, because for the laws themselves there was need of the speech that persuades. For if it is plain that the laws were to be enacted so that all might have their proper due, and that those superior in might were not going to counsel this, how was there not of necessity need already of the speech that would persuade? For it was not possible to compel those who were by nature inclined to this very thing, nor was this the origin of laws; for it was for the very sake of not using force that the laws had to be enacted. So it was not possible to enact them by force, but this would have been the first thing contrary to the laws. There was need, then, to persuade above all the very men who opposed, and at once by this very thing to make them better; or if not, at least the many, and those on whose behalf one was legislating. For the one set, using their own nature, were going to wrong the others toward the many; the other set, using both that of rhetoric and their own, were going to benefit even those, toward them — if indeed they were to be sober. But if, then, those did not accept it, it remained to persuade the many, and those on whose behalf one was legislating, of this very thing — that one was legislating on their own behalf. There was need, then, of speeches and persuasion. For this one reason, then, rhetoric is thus of necessity prior to laws and their leader. And secondly, what, by the gods, must one say the laws themselves are, but speeches — differing so much from the rest as they are written? If I remember anything, Aeschines agrees that Socrates too

bears witness. And apart from the testimony, both of Aeschines and of Socrates, one might see it by looking at the matter itself. For they tell us, in a way, both what we must do and what we must abstain from, both in peace and in war, both singly and in common, and they govern the cities continually. Therefore the things that are in the public speeches of the orators, these the laws say, except that the laws do not leave off speaking, but play the orator through all time, since, I think, they are written. When, then, the speeches about these things belong to rhetoric, the laws are a part of rhetoric. For the being written, that comes to be, is a part belonging to speeches, if indeed some are spoken from the mouth, while others are written. And surely the decrees the orators themselves compose. Therefore, when the decrees are of the same nature as the laws and of the same polities, both belong to the orators, so that the laws at least are a part of rhetoric.

Come now, let us consider also about the judicial art, for what we needed it and what it wishes for us. Or is this also the easiest of all to see, that it succours the laws? For those who transgress the things they command, these it searches out and punishes; and not even this simply, but here too it follows the laws. For as they bid, so it chastises. So be it. What, then, does the judicial art need toward these things? Whence will it find the just, except from rhetoric? For the one refutes what is done, while the other gives its vote upon the refutations. Here too, then, rhetoric appears to wish the same things as the judicial art, but to prevail by so much as it alone securely holds them both together. For the judicial art, wishing to come, as in battle, to the aid of legislation, suffered the same thing as legislation itself. For that art needed rhetoric first, so that the laws might have an entrance to it; and the judicial art, having taken the figure of an ally to the laws, itself first needed the aid that comes from rhetoric. For it had to be able to give aid; but this was not possible without rhetoric. By so much, then, is rhetoric more august

and more honourable than the judicial art, as I almost say the judge is than the executioner. For the orator refutes the crimes and hands them over to the judge, and the judge, having heard and learned, hands them over in turn to the officers, and the judge is midway between the servant and the orator. And again, when the suit has reached its end, the judicial art has nothing whatever left over, but, as legislation, having enacted the laws, is finished, so the judge is finished after the verdict. But rhetoric, taking in hand those who, either through ignorance or through ill will, are vexed at the verdicts and carry matters off into tumults or factions, restrains and admonishes them, persuading them to be content with the laws and the vote of the judges — not honouring the law of Pindar, O you who say things contrary to the nature of rhetoric, nor chanting these things: "Law, the king of all, both of mortals and immortals, leads on, justifying the most violent, with sovereign hand. I judge by the deeds of Heracles, since unbought —" For you say you do not remember the whole; and perhaps you ought not to remember even these things, at least not for rhetoric. But up to this point rhetoric too says, "Law, the king of all, both of mortals and immortals"; but what follows is no longer the same — how should it be? Day and night will never agree on the same things — but quite the contrary: it leads on, honouring justice and admonishing the bold in their insolence. For if it should think fit that the most violent be the law that justifies, and that the sovereign hand of Heracles prevail — Heracles, who along with his hand cared for justice — it will perish by its own arguments. For what place is left,

or use, for rhetoric or for speeches, if the hand defines the just and the man able to instruct about the matter shall have no advantage? And where is persuasion, if force prevails? And this, too, when she who has persuasion for her work has given force the advantage? And it seems to me that Pindar too, if one must say something about the song, did not say these things by way of proposal or counsel, in earnest, to men, but as if in indignation. "I judge by the deeds of Heracles" — by these very words; because elsewhere too, recalling these matters in a certain dithyramb, he says, "But you, Geryon, among us I do praise; yet what is not dearer to Zeus, I keep wholly silent." For it is not fitting, he says, when one's goods are being snatched away, to sit by the hearth and be a coward. And yet to fight against law — and that the king of men and of gods alike — was not a thing for Pindar to praise, nor to counsel kicking against the goads. He himself, at any rate, has called such a thing a "slippery path" and bids us beware of it. But what, he says, are these things to me now? For whether these things seemed good to Pindar or not, yet such a thing will not be shown to seem good to rhetoric. For one must not snatch each thing as one can and call this law, but each must obtain his just due, and one must honour the law that distributes these things, and call only such a thing law, and the contrary lawlessness. This is the doctrine of rhetoric, and with this law she dwells, and about this she persuades, watching that no one transgress, bringing the transgressors to soberness. And here is the greatest proof: for where there is law and justice, there too are rhetoric and speeches; but where the superior hand takes away the just, there you would see nothing administered by rhetoric. But the laws, the trial, and speeches are, as it were, of one portion and nature. There being these three powers, as I said in digressing, rhetoric alone occupies all the places. For being prior to

legislation, in respect of the need of it, and prior again to the judicial art, since that too was needed, having taken the legislative art first as the middle, and then again the judicial art likewise, enclosing each on both sides, she becomes first and middle and last — at once setting herself in the middle of both, and at once setting both in the middle of herself — so that they might most of all abide together, using rhetoric as a bond. Is rhetoric, then, "an image of a part of statecraft," or are the parts of statecraft, as you say, held together by rhetoric? For to me, in truth, he appears in these matters not to be censuring rhetoric, nor to be showing an image of a part of statecraft, but, as it were, having taken some image of rhetoric, to be busy about this, and not even to touch rhetoric herself — like the Trojans of Stesichorus, who held the image of Helen as though it were Helen herself. But he would differ so much, that the image is not even like rhetoric. But surely they say there are four parts of virtue: prudence, temperance, justice, courage. Rhetoric, then, was discovered in prudence and on behalf of justice; and temperance and courage of those who possess her save the cities — temperance, since they choose the orderly life before disorder, and courage, because they do not yield to opponents. For if they yield, they will not guard rhetoric, so that, as long as they guard her, they do not yield. Therefore it is not the case that, there being four parts of flattery, rhetoric is to justice what cookery is to medicine; rather, there being four parts of virtue, all have been wrought through her, and what gymnastic and medicine are in the body — I mean both together — that rhetoric appears to be in the soul and in the affairs of cities. For the things uncertain whether they will even come to be

she foresees, whenever she addresses the people; and the things how they may not come to be she foresees, whenever she legislates; and some things she preserves so far as she can; and the things done she sets right, whenever she hands over the wrongdoers to the judges. What, then, if Archelaus, having killed his own master and uncle, seized the rule, or, having cast that man's seven-year-old son into the well, said to Cleopatra that he had fallen in chasing a goose, or raved in some madness at the mill — what are these things to rhetoric, O you who have moved every argument and all but the very stones in truth? What do these irrelevant episodes mean for you? "For I, for my part, did not persuade these things," rhetoric would say. "Nor, if anyone obeyed me, would he have accomplished these things, or anything else whatever, by slaughtering and strangling; but, having persuaded and openly demonstrated, would have laid claim to what belonged to himself. At least in lesser matters," she says, "I use this method, and I give the inheritances not to those who have snatched them, but to those who have demonstrated their right. And Archelaus himself," she says, "I would so far from ever having thought worthy of these things, that I would straightway have brought him to where he would have paid a fair penalty — and that perhaps even before he strangled the boy, while the first murders were still in his hands — if rhetoric had had any place in Macedonia. But as it is, in my absence, he did the wrong, and they had the misfortune, both those who were destroyed and those who received such a ruler. So that, if from no other quarter, at least from the evils of Archelaus learn how fine a thing rhetoric is, and how necessary, for a city and a nation that is going to be saved, and not to be wretchedly

enslaved to the accursed." These things, I think, rhetoric would persuade more, saying things proper to herself and just and belonging to her. But if Plato thinks to refute her by these things, it is time, I think, to bring against her also the deeds of Gyges the Lydian — these are even stranger — that, having killed his master, he held the rule; and she was privy and an accomplice, being the wife of the one and the mistress of the other. Why, then, do we not also tell those tales — that Cyrus, having crossed the Araxes, joined battle with the Massagetae, and Darius, having bridged the Bosporus, crossed against the Scythians, and Xerxes, having bridged the Hellespont, against Greece, and Ninus was taken by the Medes, and Sardanapalus was burned alive, having himself mounted the pyre? And what are these things to the purpose? Or when would one cease accusing rhetoric, if all the calamities that ever befell either private men or cities he should reckon to rhetoric? And yet, about Archelaus, one might also say this: that this man was the one who called Socrates to himself, none of the orators; but I let this pass. But, I think, it is ridiculous. For as long as a man does not show rhetoric to be the cause of these things, nor these things to befall through her nature, he does not grant that rhetoric erred; and this is to refute what is in question. And besides, it is silly, if he should think it permitted to himself to attach to rhetoric all licence and the things that are not her works, but does not see the opposite argument,

nor will suppose that the man who speaks on her behalf and exalts her will be able to bring to rhetoric all the good things that were ever done among men. We, then, demonstrate for what rhetoric was discovered, so that, if this is a fine thing, we may consider rhetoric good also; but if it is shameful and to be fled, we may use the same names and reckonings about rhetoric too. She appears, then, from the beginning to have been composed and considered on behalf of justice — just as from these things, as I said, this name, "the laws," got its force. For there was need, for those worsted by the hands, of speech and of law as helper. Therefore, whatever crimes a man may pick out and bring into the midst, besides accomplishing nothing to the purpose, he will bring them as a contribution to the arguments for rhetoric, not against her. For these and such things were the very reasons she was discovered — to hate and prevent them. "By Zeus, but some who champion rhetoric play the false accuser." And by this very thing rhetoric is more august. How? Because some of those who champion medicine too have, I think, killed certain men with a drug, and perhaps another in some other way; but not on this account is medicine an evil thing, which is so far from killing men that it is, so to speak, a remedy against death, so far as in itself lies. Therefore whoever most hates and is displeased with those who kill, this man most welcomes and honours those who save. Therefore in the case of rhetoric too, if she is by nature such as to make men insolent and flatterers, then of necessity she is shameful and base and illiberal and unbefitting a good and noble man; but if she was shown forth for the sake of saving men by speech and saving the just, for the sake of this she was instituted — what medicine is in the body, this rhetoric is in the soul, as our argument proceeded onward

in order — for I now leave gymnastic aside. So that whoever most is displeased with the false accusers or flatterers, it most befits him to honour her who was instituted on behalf of the best and is a remedy against these very things. For just as the man who kills while professing medicine is not at once both a physician and a killer, but, so long as he is a physician, will in no way join in these deeds, but, even if another strikes the blow, will himself heal — but at once he both kills and has destroyed the art along with it — so here too men are not at once orators and false accusers and flatterers, but, so long as they are orators, neither of these, nor anything else shameful at all among them, nor anything near it, but they refute the wrongdoers and teach the ignorant about affairs; and at once they will be outside both these things and rhetoric. They will not, then, bring reproach upon rhetoric whenever they err. For they will err from her by just so much as they err from the just; since the pilot's art too is, I suppose, the art of saving those who sail, and yet one of those who sit at the stern might lead out into the open sea and sink it and do some other such thing. But neither must one censure the pilot's art for this, nor do men say that the pilot, by going on board, is the most opposed of all things to the safety of those who sail, nor does anyone, I think, put the scuttlers into one class with the pilots. For the pilot must, I think, know both the things that will harm the ship and the things that will preserve it, just as I think the physician too must know both the things dangerous to the body and the things that save it; but the art wishes to use the good in either case — reasonably, and according to its very name. And so far

is anyone who does mischief in these matters from preserving the name of the art, that even if he err unwillingly, Plato says, we do not use precise speech when we say that the physician erred, or the pilot. For so long as the art prevails, there is no error, for it is not possible to err according to it; for to err is not the art. Utterly, then, if a man should do on purpose the contrary of what the art wishes, this man we shall say does wrong by his share of the art, or does reproach to the art — rather, that he does double reproach to the art, but the art does not do it. And what need is there of other examples than the one of which we made mention a little before and showed Plato in agreement? The laws are surely enacted for the sake of the safety of the cities and the establishing of justice for all, and legislation, both according to him and according to us and according to all men, is to be reckoned among the good and fine things and along with justice — this very thing, the "justly," not escaping it; and Plato sets it down so even before. If, then, someone should ask us, putting it thus: "But how many have already brought forward laws that were in no way sound and had every dreadful feature? And how many have been convicted in indictments for illegal proposals? Or how many laws, being in force, have been repealed as not better to use? What, then? Will you say that legislation is not in every way a fine thing, on account of such laws, or that all the laws ever written or to be written are fine and just, since legislation must in every way be a fine thing?" Shall we say that he asks unanswerable things, and shall we cover ourselves up? Or whose is it to find a moderate answer, one that will say that legislation and the laws that truly are laws are a fine and just thing? For it was for this that they first came to men; but such things are not laws so much as, in Demosthenes' word, lawlessness, both the things the laws forbid and on whose behalf

they were discovered, that they should not come to be? And I, for my part, would add this, that "O you who ask in this way, you do not frighten me by this, that some who wrote laws have already been convicted of illegal proposals." Rather, this too bears witness for me. For those convicted of illegal proposals are no longer laws, to speak precisely; for they would not be laws and at the same time contrary to the laws. So that it befits these writings themselves to be called lawless, not lawful. Let these things be my answer, on behalf of rhetoric too, against Plato. And the answer we would then have made in common, let this now be made by me for the present case. They would not be at once both flatterers and orators, nor at once false accusers and orators, if rhetoric truly came in for the sake of justice and the safety of men, as the laws did. But so long as medicine saves the sick, and the pilot's art saves those who sail, and the laws those who use them, the speeches of rhetoric save those whom they ought, and guard the just; since even this thing called by us philosophy, if anyone wished to censure it, he could bring forward many things in his speeches — as, for instance, if he should accuse Diagoras and Anaxagoras and, picking out certain others, men who were strange either later or earlier; of whom some, I suppose, corrupted certain men, and some blasphemed about the gods, and some said certain other speeches which it would have been better not to say at all, and some brought in more self-will than prudence. But would it not be better to say thus: that, if certain men using philosophy as a screen have become base and no better than the many — or, by Zeus, even cleverer at doing mischief — philosophy is not on this account to be dishonoured, so long as philosophy is not the doing of such things, but one must use these very proofs against those men, that they have erred from philosophy.

Nor, I think, if certain men flatter or play the false accuser, does this make rhetoric worse; rather, these things must be thought to belong to men who have erred from rhetoric, just as those others from philosophy, who, under the screen of the fairest thing, procure for themselves the licence to do mischief. And it would be absurd if we shall judge the works of the cobblers and the carpenters not from the things in which they fail, but from the things in which they succeed as best may be, but rhetoric we shall judge not only not from those who accomplished her most beautifully, but even from those who do the very contraries of what rhetoric wishes. "Yes; but it is better to be wronged than to do wrong." Let this be so. Is it, then, just as it is better, so also altogether to be chosen? No. At any rate he says he wishes neither — plainly because he considers being wronged too an evil, rightly, I think, both knowing and saying it. Therefore, if Plato himself should answer us, it would be of the greatest worth to the argument. And this too is available. How? As Socrates has been made by him to answer. For the matter stands disposed thus. Polus asks Socrates, "Would you, then, wish rather to be wronged than to do wrong?" And he replies, "I, for my part, would wish neither; but if it were necessary either to be wronged or to do wrong, I would choose rather to be wronged." Therefore, when he says he wishes neither, it is plain that, considering being wronged too an evil, he says he does not wish it, but that being wronged is better than doing wrong — yet not better than that neither doing wrong nor being wronged — rightly, I think, both knowing and saying it. If, then, rhetoric prevented being wronged but compelled to do wrong, not even so, perhaps, would it be altogether evil, being evil in preventing being wronged, but worse, perhaps, than the better, if indeed being wronged is

better than doing wrong. But if it neither compels the one and prevents the other, then in respect of the one it is so far neither good nor evil — for let us grant this for the present — but in respect of the other it is properly good, and better or worse by just so much as it has partaken of the better and not of the worse, if indeed it is better neither to do wrong nor to be wronged than to do one of those two things. And surely the man who has resolved not to do wrong does not at the same time both himself abstain from mischief and escape being wronged. For this very thing was doing wrong — to treat ill the man one ought not. So that, so long as there is doing of mischief among men, he will be wronged. But the man who has the guard against being wronged at the same time also somehow prevents wrongdoing. For just as one man is at once wronged and another has done the wrong, so the man who has the power of not being wronged has the same power of not allowing wrongdoing. So that, if he sets not being wronged down as belonging to rhetoric, but not doing wrong as belonging to philosophy, philosophy is worse than rhetoric by just so much as doing wrong is worse than being wronged. But when, again, he sets before this the neither doing wrong nor being wronged, by this rhetoric in turn becomes better than philosophy, since indeed together with being wronged it does away with doing wrong also. Since the laws too, in preventing being wronged, at the same time, I suppose, prevent wrongdoing. For it is not possible, the wronged not existing, that the wrongdoers should exist, there being no one against whom this comes. So that rhetoric, in preventing being wronged, prevents wrongdoing too by the very same thing by which it prevents being wronged. But if, indeed, we are showing rhetoric to have been discovered wholly for the aid of justice, and to hold purely the same rank as the laws, then not only, as it seems, will the orator not flee being wronged while confirming the doing of wrong, but he will prevent nothing so much as the doing of wrong. For he will take thought not only for what concerns himself, but that no other man either may suffer ill, if indeed for the things for the sake of which the laws exist, for these too rhetoric has been shown to have been discovered.

But surely the man who compels others to do justice has, far and away first, prepared himself for it. For it is not possible to come to the aid of justice, while oneself being first the one to overthrow the just. Therefore the orator will not only not do wrong himself, but he will not permit another either; nor, again, will he only not be wronged himself, but no other either, so far as in him lies. And if he will neither do wrong nor permit another, then in every way rhetoric is a fine and noble thing — both by that account by which doing wrong is shameful, and by that by which being wronged is better than doing wrong, and by that by which it is altogether best neither to do wrong nor to be wronged; and the man who is truly an orator has been shown to be, simply to say, so much better than a good man, by as much as the one furnishes only what concerns himself, while the other prepares others too to become such. For the good and noble man is not in every way an orator, but the orator is a good and noble man, who indeed leads others too to these things. But if, indeed, Plato insists on this, that rhetoric provides no great use, nor one worthy of earnest or of speech, because being wronged is not so great an evil as doing wrong, what prevents him from striking out all the laws too by these same arguments? For they wish nothing else than this: most of all that no one suffer ill from anyone, but if not, that justice come to those who have suffered from those who did it or were responsible. So that not only does rhetoric depart from the cities, banished by Plato, but, as though a club had been condemned, she will be driven out along with the laws that have the same wishes; and then we will send rhetoric away and revile her, when it is well for us to send the laws away along with her. When, then, would this come to be? What is the occasion

for it? Let one of Plato's companions answer, since we cannot bring himself forward. And surely not even here will he stand for us wholly outside testimony, but he appears bearing witness even more in these passages than in those he has just gone through. "For I will not discourse about the other laws and constitutions, nor about those which so-and-so enacted; but" — if anyone should ask him: "O divine man, you who discover all wonderful things, if being wronged is no matter, and the power that prevents this is worth no account, nor all that it is and does any good thing, but so dishonourable and illiberal as to be a part of flattery and of shadow, for what reason, in founding this city in the book, do you set up for it a constitution from which it shall suffer nothing whatever, and bid the warlike class be settled apart from the rest, assigning it the first honour, that the city may suffer nothing, nor be wronged by any kind of enemies? For if it sufficed not to do wrong, what do you fear, if you have prepared the city at least for this? And if, indeed, it is worse for the wrongdoers when they do not pay the penalty, and one must, according to you, become accuser even of oneself whenever one does wrong, and of one's children and one's own father, but leave one's enemies alone — why do you not pray together with the enemies that they come upon you and take the city, and, by Zeus, cut down all of military age, and that too at the altars, and lead away into slavery children and women beyond, if you please, Gadeira, and, having plundered the temples, raze them all, and not even leave the tombs unharmed by their greed, that, having done the greatest wrongs, they may be among the greatest evils in not paying the penalty? But you are so far from joining in these things that you prevent them, you take offence, you have devised a life in arms, that nothing of the kind may happen; and if any traitor arise among you, this man you bid not crown nor proclaim, but you think the same about these things as the rest of men. And yet, according to these arguments, whom rather than the

traitors ought one to honour, because they prepare their own people and the country and the temples and all that is, to be under the enemy, that those men, having done the greatest wrongs, may be entangled in the greatest evils? Tell me, by Zeus of portents, what must we think about these things?" So be it, O noble man; and why, again, did you enact for us so many laws besides — laws that fix honours for those who have lived well, and tell what those who do any wrong must suffer? And you play the orator about each of them in earnest, and honour the preambles, and set forth a double pattern, like the modellers — you who despise speeches. For if, my friend, taking justice and not permitting wrongdoing were not one of the earnest things, for what reason do you busy yourself with these and consider how no one may be wronged? Therefore either all these things, so many in number, must be in error, this one of them being right, or else those things stand refuted by these. And surely, in the things we say, there is the consent of others too, and Plato besides; but the things he has said here are refuted not only by the arguments of the matters, but also by Plato's own arguments and wishes. Those things, then, being agreed to be right, both the opinion of the rest bears witness and the vote is correct; but if we should grant these things to prevail, the consenting of any of the rest is absent. And it is stronger to have the consent of all, and of Plato, than the consent of none, and not even of Plato, as he elsewhere says. Therefore we shall not flee the testimony from him on account of that from the rest, but to that of the rest we shall add the testimony from him.

I hold, then, that in these things too I furnish the testimony of fact. For to contend with speeches against speeches, and to declare one's opponent to be bearing witness to other earnest speeches, is to furnish the testimony of fact. But nevertheless I wish to go still further, so that, since he honours the putting of a single matter to the vote, even by him against whom the speeches are made, I may show him to be on my side both in word and in deed. Come, then, let there be added in these matters too a question, as if someone asked him, when he was sailing to Sicily the second or third time, whether as a fellow-voyager or even as the pilot himself: "But you, O Plato, for what reason do you sail to Sicily?" Or, if not then, yet if someone, when he had returned home, asked him the causes of his journey and wandering, and what indeed he suffered that a third time he busied himself about Charybdis — around which Odysseus passed not more than twice — what would he have answered him? For if we grant that the best is true — as Plato must grant — there is left him about the matters in dispute no other answer than this. Why? Because, I think, he would say — or rather he did say — that he sailed for the sake of Dion, a companion and guest-friend, wishing to settle his affairs with Dionysius and not to overlook them. Then, O you who sail well and go abroad justly, you, for the sake of a Syracusan guest-friend, a common enemy of your own fatherland — for there was no seat of honour for Athenians at Syracuse, but things which one cannot even speak of without tears, these the companions and fellow-citizens of Dion had suffered at their hands a little while before — yet, since once you received him as a friend, considering him so, you sailed for his sake in your old age over so great a sea, and that too to a man at whose hands you would again have to be in danger, and whose offered alliance you knew your own fatherland had not received; and you did not flee the seeming to consort with a tyrant, as having for consolation the figure of your pursuit, which was that Dion should remain at home and keep control of his property. But when a man, dwelling in his own land and among his own

fellow-citizens and parents and brothers, has the guard so that they shall not be wronged, and saves both them and himself — and, by Zeus, if he is able to prevent this very thing, a man who is going to become a tyrant and like Dionysius, and to take away by speech his deeds and to confirm for all the security that comes from the laws — shall we then say that this is no earnest matter, and that one ought not to praise such a thing, whether one must call it an art or not an art, because, by Zeus, this one thing was a great evil, doing wrong, while being wronged was no matter at all? Does one, then, even more greatly defend oneself against one's enemy by allowing him to do wrong, and by considering by what means no other either shall take justice from him? And surely, up to these arguments one might say that these things are riddles; but these having been brought forward — and by Plato — and both refuted and resolved, not in the customary and same manner as other riddles, becoming clear from unclear, but truly clear as to where the rottenness of them lay. Come, then, let us consider these things too. For I think we have, as it were, the deposition of an absent witness. It is from the long Letter. "With this purpose and daring I set out from home — not the purpose some supposed, but ashamed before myself, most of all, lest I should ever seem to myself to be simply and wholly a mere word, and never willingly to lay hold of any deed; and lest I should risk betraying, first, the guest-friendship and companionship of Dion, who was truly in no small dangers. If, then, he should suffer anything, or, cast out by Dionysius and his other enemies, should come to us in exile and ask, saying, 'O Plato, I have come to you an exile, not wanting hoplites nor lacking horsemen to ward off

my enemies, but wanting speeches and persuasion, by which I knew you above all able, turning young men toward good and just things, to establish them each time in friendship and companionship with one another. For want of these, on your part, I have now left Syracuse and am here. And the lesser reproach it brings to you; but philosophy, which you always praise and say is dishonoured by the rest of men — how is it not now betrayed, so far as in you lies, along with me? And if we happened to be dwelling in Megara, you would surely have come to my aid in the things to which I summoned you, or you would have thought yourself the basest of all men; but as it is, do you think that, by pleading the length of the journey and the greatness of the voyage and the toil, you will ever escape a reputation for baseness? Far from it.' When these things had been said, what fitting answer should I have had against them? There is none." These things no other has written about him, nor conjecturing his judgment, but he who best knew, himself about himself, says he came for the sake of these things, ashamed at the words which Dion might have spoken to him. And I, for my part, believe it; for I should be mad if I did not. Therefore in these passages there is: "I have come to you, O Plato, not wanting hoplites nor bereft of horsemen, but of speeches and persuasion; and these I thought, more than anything, to be with you." Finely indeed, O Plato, both saying this yourself and thinking that Dion would say it to you. Therefore, if to be cast out or to suffer anything was for Dion conspicuously a dreadful thing, but to act so that he should not be cast out a fine and just thing, and, being so disposed, he needed speeches and persuasion, while you sailed because you had these — you have agreed to everything: both that one must be earnest that someone, so far as is possible, may not be wronged; and that the power of speeches to persuade is not a paltry thing; and that those who persuade about these things are worthy not only of praise among men, but also blameless before the gods,

if indeed those who fall short are not even holy. And further, you have done a still greater thing in every way, if indeed not only a people, nor judges, but even tyrants one must not flee from persuading otherwise about these things, and at so great a distance abroad. The whole Letter, then — for the sake of what did he write it, or of persuasion? And surely the matter itself shows it, and Plato himself in many places of the Letter. For both the going through the things for the sake of which he came, and the further agreement that he goes through them in order that he may establish the true opinion about himself, are the work of one who persuades. Therefore he both wrote it that he might persuade, and, in writing, says that he went away for the sake of persuading, lest Dion should suffer anything bereft of speeches. How, then, do the orators do shameful things? Or by which of these is rhetoric a paltry thing? Is it by that by which it is naturally fit to aid the wronged, even if some ill repute and danger attend it? But that one must despise persuading by speech? But you yourself, as one who would persuade by speech, say you ran a risk in deed. "And if we happened to be dwelling in Megara," Dion says to you, "you would surely have come to my aid in the things to which I summoned you, or you would have thought yourself the basest of all men; but as it is, do you think that, by pleading the length of the journey and the greatness of the voyage and the toil, you will ever escape a reputation for baseness? Far from it." What, then, if someone, turning it about thus, should say to you yourself: "And do you think one must sail to Sicily and suffer anything whatever for the sake of persuading someone that one of one's intimates ought to remain at home; but if a man, not even so far as from Athens to Megara, but not even needing to go anywhere at all, but staying at home, handles the power of saving his own people thereby, do you not think this man has escaped all reputation for baseness? Long ago, even by your own showing, if indeed any of the things said before are of any use." How, then, shall the man who does not aid by speech at once bear a reputation for baseness, and at once the man who does aid not escape a reputation for baseness? You do not, then, say this when you call rhetoric, to which these things belong, flattery.

"What fitting answer should I have had against these things?" he says. And to the things we now ask, what answer, by the gods? But I wish to make a small distinction, lest anyone suppose at all that I am accusing Plato by these arguments, or speaking ill with an occasion at hand. For I myself neither make it a charge, I suppose, if Plato thought he ought to go anywhere and in any way for any cause whatever, nor do I think the man who brings forward any such thing to be of sound mind, nor do I busy myself at all with anything outside what comes to the argument — let no prize be worth so much — but the things he himself did and for the sake of which he did them, which he himself has clearly stated, these I say accord with the arguments on behalf of rhetoric; and I am so far from reproaching him by these things that, if one must say this too, even in these very things I think to exalt him, if, these things being contrary to those, I do not slander his deeds and acts, but, from his life and works which are on our side and which we deem worthy of being, I show that those words of his stand otherwise than one might believe. When, then, he saw Dion preparing and acting so that he might take justice for what he had suffered, does he appear writing to him to let it go and count it as nothing, and that, if he hates Dionysius and supposes him ill-disposed, he must overlook it and consent that, doing the greatest wrongs, he be among the extreme evils — or, far the contrary, urging him on and thinking fit that he be assiduous, that he might have as many as possible to act with him against that man; and setting down Dionysius as in every way an enemy, counselling him to consider how he will defend himself, and himself joining in the work so far as in him lay, only declining to sail and campaign with him — because, since Dionysius, having him, had then felt shame and not killed him, it was not

fitting to go against that man? And yet, if one ought to let one's enemies, and those one hates beyond measure, go on doing wrong, and rhetoric, which makes one take justice from them and does not let them proceed as far as they can, is paltry and useless, then he ought surely most of all to have prevented Dion — being his companion and pupil — and to have reminded him of what he once heard, if he did hear it; or, if not, then at least to teach him on the spot, by the facts, that he must bear in silence and consider how not only he himself shall be deprived of his fatherland and his property by Dionysius, but also many others shall suffer these and other such things to the end, and Dionysius shall not cease wronging all men; and to pray with him that Dionysius become tyrant not only of Sicily, but also of Carthage and Libya, if possible, and, by Zeus, of all Europe, and, if there were any device, of Asia too; and that he himself not only consider nothing about the overthrow of the tyrant, but that no one else either attack him, either to kill him or to cast him out, but, on the contrary, take thought for the guarding of Dionysius' person, that the wretch might be immortal, and, wronging all men in all things, be in all evils at all times. These things, most of all, he ought to have taught Dion beforehand and admonished him, if he trusted these arguments; or, if not, at least to appear not joining in his deliberation about vengeance — which, far from doing, he has become for us a witness in deed about the things we doubted, that he does not talk nonsense. I wish, then, to show him bearing witness, in a way, with his whole household. For Socrates, drawn up in line at Potidaea, and again at Delium, retreating when the rout occurred, plainly to all even from very far off, that whoever should lay hold of this man would defend himself most vigorously — how is this man not clearly bearing witness that one must not allow those who

attempt to do wrong? No one, surely, will gainsay it. For it is not the things he said later — when he thought it already timely to die, and that it was hard to do away with the many slanders gathered from long ago and by many — that are the strong proofs of his judgment, but the things he plainly did when he was not in a position to prevent. Wherefore indeed he too, and his companion, retired safely, he says: "for they hardly even touch such men in war, but pursue rather those who flee headlong." For this much more has accrued to him from these things, that again, with the Socrates of Plato, Plato himself bears witness to the argument: "such men they do not much touch, but pursue rather those who flee headlong." Clearly, then, in the cities too, those who watch for such things do not much touch the men so disposed as to defend themselves, but pursue those who yield. So that, if it is reasonable to praise the brave in wars, then the men of this sort here too. So that, if for no other reason, on account of the false accusers rhetoric is a fine thing. And surely, if men do not dare to wrong such persons, both good results follow, and consistent with the arguments just made — that he himself is not wronged, and that he does not allow another to be wronged. And he who went up even to the plain of Babylon with Cyrus, when he was marching against his brother who had first done wrong — Xenophon — how is not he too, of his own household, a witness for us to Plato in the present arguments? For one cannot say this: that in arms, and on behalf of others' interests, it is reasonable to defend oneself against those who attempt to do

wrong, but if a man should do this same thing by speech, to disparage it, even if he proceed on behalf of what he himself has suffered; nor, still less, can one say this: that to defend oneself with arms belongs to the fitting things for those who have lived in speeches, but that to defend oneself by the very speeches must be set down as unreason. No one would say these things. And surely, by as much as prudence is finer than courage, by so much is rhetoric finer than valour in war. For, if one must put it in sum, rhetoric is nothing else than prudence that has taken to itself the power of speeches, so that one may not only oneself do the best things, but also be able to persuade others. I hold, then, that these things too have proofs of the truth sufficient — if not, indeed, more than sufficient.

But I go now to the very colophon, as one might say, of Plato's words. For I wish him to appear bearing witness not only from the things by which he is refuted, but as if, standing beside us, he himself bore witness with his own voice: "For those who live happily it is necessary first to do no wrong to others and to be wronged by none. Of these two, the one is not very hard, but to acquire the power of not being wronged is wholly hard; and it is not possible to have this perfectly otherwise than by becoming perfectly good." Hurrah, hurrah for the testimony! These are the things I needed. Plato says these things — the partner in the epigram, and through whom the race of Ariston is truly divine. Perfectly, then, O divine man, rhetoric is a fine thing, and not for everyone either to take or to possess. For you appear to grant this too, that it is ranged on the side of not being wronged. Therefore, when it did not compel doing wrong, but did not permit being wronged — and, as followed from the argument, permits neither of these, neither doing wrong nor being wronged —

then, if the definition of philosophy too is the same, rhetoric appears to be a kind of philosophy. But if it suffices for philosophy not to do wrong, rhetoric is more perfect; for it adds the harder thing to acquire, and the greater — that he himself shall not be wronged by others. How, then, is the same thing at once perfectly good and the greatest of goods, and at once the extreme of evils and flattery? And how do the orators have the least power, if indeed that of which it is wholly hard to acquire the power is theirs in abundance? I, for my part, cannot reconcile it. Happy, then, not wretched, by Plato's argument, are the orators, if indeed the perfectly good man is happy, and this is not possible to acquire without becoming perfectly good. Then he wishes to refute rhetoric, but he accuses the tyrants and the dynasts, mixing things that do not mix, as if Heracles — may the example be gracious — having been ordered to slay the lion in Nemea, then, grappling with an ass and throttling it, thought he was strangling the lion and doing the very thing he set out to do. But the example falls so far short, that this man does not put one thing in the place of another in using such argument, but even falls into the contraries. For who does not know that rhetoric and tyranny are as far apart from one another as persuading is from compelling? And surely no one would be ashamed to say that these things have a contrary nature. So that, if to use force and to grasp for more is dreadful, then to persuade and to champion justice is fine and fitting. Therefore rhetoric is not so much an evil as tyranny is; rather, if tyranny is an evil, rhetoric is a good thing from the same considerations; for the one everywhere seeks to use force, while the other has honoured persuading. So that he does the like, in thinking to refute that, as if someone

blaming the darkness in the night should think he was accusing the other strange features of the day. And at one moment he says rhetoric is flattery, and again he sets the dynasts and the orators in the same class — not only saying that neither belongs to this power, but, besides its not belonging, that it is entirely alien to it; nay, even putting together two charges that are the very contraries. For how do the orators at once flatter, and at once stand among the dynasts? For the flatterers, surely the greatest and most perfect of them, are wholly the servants of the tyrants themselves; and there are some, I think, of ordinary men too; so that what a slave is toward a master, that a flatterer is toward a tyrant. But the tyrants, on the other hand, are so far from flattering that they thrust all aside by force, and one cannot obtain even moderate things from them, much less the service that is beyond what is fitting; so that the tyrant has all but exceeded even the measure of the master. For nothing is more abject than a flatterer, nor more given to choosing to be a slave; but nothing could you call more savage than a tyrant, nor more given to wishing to play the master. So that, if rhetoric is flattery, the charges against the tyrants do not concern her; but if she is with tyranny, she has exceeded flattery by great bounds. Therefore the one set or the other is altogether already false. For me, then, even if I had nothing good to say about her, this is enough — if I show that even thus he does not speak the truth; but for him, even if he has rightly brought the other charge, the argument about the other is not left. But surely, that he does not rightly bring both at once, he is refuted by his own arguments clashing together; and that he does neither rightly, we have just now shown — privately showing that it is not flattery, and again that it does not share with tyranny. How, then, is he not thrice defeated — both by the argument of the two together,

and by that of each separately? And the same thing is preserved for us in all. For about both together he is thrust aside by his own arguments, and again, in respect of each, he bears witness himself in turn — both by the fact that persuading appeared with him to be one of the useful things, and by the fact that, accusing those who use force and are insolent, he is seen doing so throughout the whole argument. For rhetoric is as far separated from tyranny as — if one must say this too — Plato from Dionysius. It is possible, then, to learn both from the matter itself and from what has befallen, how great is the difference of each of these, and according to how great a necessity it is. For it will appear that neither, where rhetoric is preserved, does a tyrant arise so long as it is preserved by speech, nor, again, does rhetoric survive where tyranny prevails; but the orator does everything so that no tyrant may arise, foreseeing at once his own and the common good, that no one, having taken from him the persuading-by-speech, may himself lead affairs by violence at the start; and the tyrants, considering and fearing nothing of all things more than lest someone arise able to speak and persuade, who, gathering the multitudes and becoming a counsellor and informer of what is fitting, may at once render their rule and their licence void. For this very reason they have necessarily their enmity toward one another; for the safety and power of the one set is, at the start, the not-being of the other. So that how much would the orators give, if one might so say, that someone should appear for them, as in battle — Plato, I say, or anyone whatever as helper and ally — to bring the evils of the tyrants into the midst and show them, and not even by night to cease speaking ill of them. For he who shows these things will all but spend and display the very speeches of rhetoric, and in a certain way the aid will come to the orators from their own household. And those again who desire to be tyrants — how much would they give that the tribe of orators in the cities should be disbelieved, and supposed flatterers and no better than cooks —

those who attempt to persuade by speech — that the proverb may not in vain say to "reap the deserts." Then, the things that profit those who attempt to do wrong — how can these be conceded to those who honour justice? "How, then, do the orators say things contrary to one another?" — This is no longer among the things said by Plato; nevertheless, for the sake of cleansing the argument on every side, let not even this be left by us unexamined, and that too being virtually the strongest of all, as among the falsehoods which that man has stated. — Because, I think, we encounter even ourselves in our arguments, this very thing which I too have now done; but the original argument is none the more destroyed by it, since those said to philosophize too do not, I suppose, all use the same arguments, but even the most contrary to one another. But nothing prevents philosophy from being a fine thing in respect of those who attain the truth; it is not, I suppose, double or contrary to itself. How, then, would one say? Shall we say that both philosophize who say contrary things? Or that philosophizing is a fine thing in the way I said? And you might see pilots too fighting at sea against one another; but nonetheless it belongs to the pilot's art to save the ship. So, then, even when the orators say things contrary to one another, as one might put it, the original chief point of rhetoric is not hindered, but one must consider what results from the argument, remembering for what it was discovered. This, then, is the argument on behalf of rhetoric.

But since he laid hold also of Miltiades and Themistocles and Cimon and Pericles, saying that they did not champion the city toward the best — there is perhaps nothing pressing now to dispute about these men. For these men, if Plato has accused them justly, would justly be considered base; but rhetoric, even if we should set these men down as the most worthless of all, is no more refuted thereby. We granting this, then, the argument on behalf of rhetoric is not lost. But if, indeed, even about these men he should be refuted as not having used the argument altogether fair-mindedly, he will be shown to be contentious on every side. This, then, is to the purpose, to speak about these men too. Come, then, by Zeus, if somehow, rising up or taking perception — as Dion is supposed by Plato to be speaking to the Syracusans — they should say these things to him: "We, O Plato, did the city of the Athenians no other good thing; for we were not knowers of your virtue and wisdom, and the gods do not give all things to all; but the things that came to us — goodwill, eagerness, faith, courage, such things — we furnished, so as to leave no surpassing to another, in such crises, O Plato, in which it was, in the prevailing, at once glory and safety and the things from our prayers, but, being worsted, not even to exist at all. And when we had taken these reckonings, and the gods graciously joining in the work, free was your fatherland and ours, and safe and unscathed from the insolence and lawlessness of the barbarians, and free too all Greece; and there came to be licence both for you to philosophize and for your companions, and to sail freely wherever you wished, and to have memory of us — and then, it was fair-minded, as for the better. For if then we, giving up, had handed ourselves over to the barbarians without a fight, what account of us would there have been among men? But neither did we ourselves suffer any such thing, nor did we endure that the others should, nor

did we flatter either side — neither the King, by reason of either of these, fear or hope of gain, nor again the people of the Athenians. For it was not possible, if we wished to flatter, to save them, nor did the occasion then offer the saying of anything toward pleasure for them to hear; but we were so far from being flatterers of the multitude that, even if we had wished to flatter, it was not possible. But neither did we choose it, nor was it possible, nor did we save Greece thus, by gratifying and beguiling — like those harpers you mention — but by rousing, teaching, ourselves becoming an example to the rest of how one must endure in the very terrors and the heights of the dangers, displaying, if you grant the word, our own virtue. Why, then, do you reproach us with flattery and servility — you who, having agreed that those who do not pay back the cost of their rearing privately would be base, yourself pay us no fair return for the common salvation and rearing of the Greeks, in which both you and the rest, on account of us, have been reared in freedom?" If the men should say these things, by unrolling what labyrinths of wisdom, or by saying what of all things, would one be able to gainsay them? For all men have a prior right to speak against these things rather than Plato. Why? Because in these very things which he has written to the companions of Dion, and in which Dion, dead, is supposed by him to speak as though breathing, there are these words: "But, having received such laws, since danger holds Sicily, and you neither prevail sufficiently nor again are sufficiently overpowered, it would perhaps be just and profitable for us all to cut the matter in the middle, both for you who flee

the harshness of the rule, and for those again who love to attain rule." Whose ancestors saved the greatest thing — the Greeks from the barbarians — so that it is now possible to make speeches about a constitution; but had they then perished, neither speech nor hope would have been left anywhere at all. "But of us," they would say, "not our ancestors, but we ourselves, by our own deeds and counsels and speeches, saved the Greeks from the barbarians — not the part of them dwelling in Sicily, but all of them together, and those reckoned the one half of the whole inhabited world, from the time when, raising themselves against the barbarians, they thrust them back, so that it is now possible for you to make speeches about a constitution, and even about us ourselves; but had they then perished, neither speech nor hope would have been left anywhere at all." "Now, then," Dion says, "let there be for the one freedom under a kingly rule, and for the other a responsible kingly rule, the laws being masters both of the other citizens and of the kings themselves, if they do anything lawless. And over all these, with guileless and sound mind, with the gods set up a king: first my own son, for the sake of a double gratitude, that from me and that from my father — for he freed the city from the barbarians in that time, and I from tyrants now twice, of which you yourselves have become witnesses. Second, make king the one who possesses the same name as my father, son of Dionysius, for the sake both of the present aid and of his holy character; who, having been born of a tyrant father, willingly frees the city, gaining for himself and his race an everlasting honour instead of an ephemeral and unjust tyranny. And third, one must invite to become king of Syracuse, willing of the willing city, the one now commander of the enemy's camp, Dionysius son of Dionysius, if he is willing of his own accord to pass into a king's estate — fearing the chances, and pitying

his fatherland and the neglect of the temples and the tombs, lest through contentiousness he utterly lose all things, becoming a thing of joy to the barbarians." If, then, it is reasonable that even such gifts should be received by the descendants of those who freed the city — so that they themselves become dynasts and kings instead of those former ones — surely it is just that those who themselves freed the whole race of the Greeks should, besides being deemed worthy of nothing more, not even be allowed to seem to be free as a body. And if, indeed, it is just to make the very commander of the enemy's camp a king, if he is willing to pity his fatherland and the neglect of the temples and the tombs, and that he may not through contentiousness utterly lose all things, becoming a thing of joy to the barbarians — where shall we place those who ranged themselves not with the enemy, but against the enemies from all the earth, who, besides their own fatherland, set straight the fatherlands of many others too, and preserved temples and tombs, and none of whom became a thing of joy to the barbarians, nor did Greece on their account? Are these things paltry, or worthy of paltry gratitude, for the men? Then, those whom — if one must obey Plato's words — one must think fit to honour, and that with much greater honours than the customary, shall we, persuaded by Plato's words, call flatterers and servants and worth nothing? We should not, surely, do justice.

But the strangest thing of all is that he uses these men in his refutation that rhetoric is flattery, as being orators, but again he himself releases them from flattery. For he says they did not use it in the passages where he speaks about what they suffered. In these too, then, one of the two must be false. For if rhetoric is flattery, these men must in every way be flatterers, being orators, as he says; but if

these men in no way belong to flattery, where is rhetoric flattery on their account, or what need was there of these examples? And I thought this too was not just — that, examining their purposes, one should take into account the calamities they met with. For it is not, if they did not turn out according to their wish, that they have become base, but if they did not counsel the best things for affairs. For the one is to accuse fortune, the other to refute the judgment. Come, did you, O Plato, champion toward the best either the Athenians, or any other people of those among the Greeks or the barbarians? Of those, one would gladly say. You could not say it; for you did not champion any at all. And what of your teacher and companion Socrates? Not he either. And what of Speusippus or Chaerephon? You would not say it. Is it, then, possible to declare a people good and blameless and just once for all, or is this not even possible to assert of a man? And surely, if it is possible, why in the world did you not yourself demonstrate it, nor appear, in the very deeds, a better citizen than we? But if it is impossible, why do you reproach us if we even stumbled in something, they would say again, and why do you demand an accounting of impossible things? For we were so much more profitable to the people than you, in that you neither said nor did anything worse or better, but simply shrank back; while we, so far as in us lay, did not give up, but, as a full contribution of money, we furnished to the fatherland that which comes from reckonings and speeches, and neither shrank from the multitude of those who would say the contrary, nor feared the strength of the rich, with whom he who acts on behalf of the common good must necessarily clash, nor judges, nor dangers, nor those at home, nor those abroad against the enemy, nor at all the things of

fortune and the uncertainties of the future. Which things to flee is, surely, easier for anyone than to undertake. But if all should reckon this in their necessities, the affairs of the cities are gone. These things, I think, they would say, speaking moderately, as I think. So be it. What if they did not declare the Athenians the best once for all, but better in some way? What if they would have erred more greatly both about these and about others, had they not been restrained by those men's words? Then you say the physician would die of starvation, if he should contend against the cook before children or such men as cannot recognize the truth; but if Miltiades and Cimon and Pericles, leading affairs toward the best, even stumbled in some things, at this do you wonder?
